############ Counterfactual_Algorithm/README.md ############
# Counterfactual_Algorithm — MIMIC-IV Latent World Model · Simulator · Benchmark · Offline RL

A **research environment** for intervention-conditioned patient-trajectory modeling on MIMIC-IV.
One core artifact — a **latent world model of patient dynamics** — drives three outputs: a
**simulator** (rollouts under interventions), a **counterfactual/stability benchmark**, and a
**Gym-style offline-RL environment**.

> ⚠️ **NOT a clinical tool.** All rollouts are *learned simulations from observational data*. The
> system does **not** recover true causal effects and makes **no** counterfactual-validity claims.
> Offline RL trains **inside the learned simulator only** — never a deployment claim. Metrics target
> stability / consistency / calibration, not clinical benefit.

## Pipeline & status (validated end-to-end on the MIMIC-IV demo, 100 patients)

| Stage | Script | Status | Headline result |
|------|--------|--------|-----------------|
| 0 · CLMBR smoke | `notebooks/clmbr_smoke.ipynb` | ✅ | clmbr-t-base (FEMRModel) loads + runs → **(3, 768)** representations |
| 1 · Preprocess | `preprocessing/build_trajectories.py` | ✅ | 100 patients, 107,752 events; action vocab (PCI/CABG/vasopressor/…) |
| 2a · Encoder (GRU) | `training/train_encoder.py` | ✅ | next-event val NLL 7.88 → 5.36; 256-d states |
| 2b · Encoder (CLMBR) | `models/encode_clmbr.py` | 🟡 wired+validated to the ontology step; **needs Athena vocab** | MIMIC→MEDS ✅, nested-schema ✅, 768-d frozen clmbr-t-base |
| 3 · World model | `training/train_world_model.py` | ✅ | val MSE **0.00637 < persistence 0.01038** |
| 4 · Simulator | `simulation/rollout.py` | ✅ | branching + counterfactual-pair rollouts |
| 5 · Benchmark | `benchmark/intervention_tests.py` | ✅ | swap-div 8.16; stability smooth; 128-step stable |
| 6 · Offline RL | `training/train_agent.py` | ✅ | BC return **3.74** > random 3.02 (≈ no-op 3.71) |

Outputs land in `data/` (artifacts) and `outputs/` (`benchmark_results.json`, `agent_results.json`).

## Architecture

```
events (MIMIC-IV)
   │  preprocessing/  → per-patient chronological trajectories + grouped action vocab a_t
   ▼
ENCODER  models/encoder.py     s_t = encoder(x_≤t)         [EncoderBase]
   ├─ GRUEncoder       from-scratch CLMBR-style next-event SSL (default, 256-d) ── runs anywhere
   └─ CLMBRFemrEncoder frozen StanfordShahLab/clmbr-t-base via femr (768-d) ───── target encoder
   ▼
WORLD MODEL  models/world_model.py   s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, Δt)   (deterministic | gaussian | mdn)
   ▼
SIMULATOR  simulation/rollout.py     rollout / branch / counterfactual_pair
   ├─► BENCHMARK  benchmark/{intervention_tests,metrics}.py   (Tasks 1–4)
   └─► RL ENV     rl_env/mimic_env.py + training/train_agent.py  (BC now, CQL scaffold)
DECODER  models/decoder.py   s_t → proxy outcomes (mortality / ICU / LOS) for reward + divergence
```

Swapping GRU↔CLMBR is a config switch (`encoder.kind: gru | clmbr`); everything downstream reads the
latent dim from config.

## Environment (Sherlock, el7 / glibc 2.17)

Two `$SCRATCH` venvs built with **`uv`** on a self-contained CPython 3.11 (femr 0.2.3 needs py>3.9;
torch 2.1.2 has no cp312 wheel; the cluster ships only py 3.6/3.9/3.12/3.14):

- `envs/cfa311` — lean torch-only env for the **GRU pipeline** (torch 2.1.2 + numpy/pandas/pyyaml).
- `envs/clmbr311` — heavy **CLMBR** env (`torch==2.1.2 femr==0.2.3 datasets==2.15.0
  xformers==0.0.23.post1 transformers==4.35.2`), with `pyarrow/pyzmq/scipy/scikit-learn` pinned to
  el7-compatible wheel versions to avoid Rust/OpenBLAS source builds.

# Revised plan — stochastic dynamics + co-evolving benchmarks

Incorporates two mentor corrections:
- **(b) The benchmark is coupled to the model.** Upstream phases change downstream ones; benchmark
  numbers are only valid for the exact pipeline that produced them and must be re-derived (and made
  comparable across encoders) whenever anything upstream changes.
- **(c) The dynamics are stochastic**, not a deterministic control system. The world model must emit
  a distribution; rollouts, benchmarks, and RL must all be distributional/risk-aware.

This plan changes Stages 3–6 and the engineering around them. **Nothing here is run until approved.**

---

## Principle 1 — Stochastic by default (mentor remark c)

| Stage | Current (wrong) | Revised |
|---|---|---|
| World model | deterministic MLP, point `s_{t+1}`, MSE | **Gaussian/MDN head is the default**; train by NLL; predict `p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t,Δt)`. Optional **ensemble** (seeds / MC-dropout) for epistemic uncertainty. |
| Simulator | single trajectory | **Monte-Carlo rollouts**: sample K trajectories per action plan → trajectory *distribution*. |
| Counterfactual contrast | point difference of two rollouts | **distribution of outcome differences** with credible intervals; effect reported as interval, never a point. |
| Benchmark | point MSE / single divergence | **calibration + sharpness** of the predictive distribution; divergence judged against the model's own stochastic spread (below). |
| RL | single-rollout return | **expected return over MC rollouts + risk measure (CVaR)**; policies compared as return *distributions*. |

**Key new stochastic-aware metric (also solves scale problem, see Principle 2):**
> **Intervention signal-to-noise (ISN)** = (between-arm divergence) ÷ (within-arm MC spread).
> "Does changing the treatment move the state *more than the model's own stochastic noise*?" ISN is
> dimensionless, so it's comparable across encoders, and it only credits an effect that exceeds
> intrinsic stochasticity — directly answering "this isn't a deterministic control system."

**Distinguish stochastic spread from instability** (fixes the old drift test):
- *Healthy stochastic*: bounded ensemble variance, stable mean.
- *Collapse*: variance → 0 **and** mean static.
- *Instability*: variance or mean-norm explodes.
Report mean-norm growth **and** ensemble-variance growth separately.

---

## Principle 2 — Benchmarks co-evolve with the model (mentor remark b)

**The problem we're fixing:** "swap divergence 8.16" is in GRU-256 latent units; it is meaningless
for CLMBR-768 and invalid the moment the encoder, world model, deconfounding, or data changes.

**Fix A — scale-free metrics** so encoders/world-models are comparable:
- Normalize all latent distances by per-dimension std (or `√d`) of the encoded states.
- Prefer **relative** quantities: ISN (above), coverage (calibration), fraction-on-manifold,

###### world_model.py ######
"""Stage 4 (core) — intervention-conditioned latent dynamics.

    s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, Δt)

Predicts a residual Δs (s_{t+1} = s_t + Δs), which stabilizes multi-step rollouts. Three heads
behind one module:

  * deterministic : MLP -> Δs.                         (default; trains today)
  * gaussian      : MLP -> (Δs mean, log-var); NLL.    (stochastic; trains today)
  * mdn           : mixture-density head.              (scaffold — structure only)

CAVEAT: this is a learned dynamics model fit to observational transitions. It does NOT recover
true causal effects; rollouts are simulations conditioned on the action embedding, to be judged on
stability/consistency, not clinical validity.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

from models.deconfound import grad_reverse


def dt_features(dt_hours: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Cheap, bounded time-gap features from Δt in hours."""
    dt = dt_hours.clamp(min=0).float()
    return torch.stack([torch.log1p(dt), (dt / 24.0).clamp(max=30.0)], dim=-1)


class WorldModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim: int, n_actions: int, cfg: dict):
        super().__init__()
        wm = cfg["world_model"]
        self.kind = wm["kind"]
        self.latent_dim = latent_dim
        a_dim = wm["action_embed_dim"]
        d_dim = wm["dt_embed_dim"]
        self.action_emb = nn.Embedding(n_actions, a_dim)
        self.dt_proj = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, d_dim), nn.ReLU())

        # Optional CRN-style balancing adapter (deconfounding). Off by default => identical to the
        # plain conditional dynamics model, so prior runs are unaffected.
        dc = cfg.get("deconfound", {}) or {}
        self.balance = bool(dc.get("enabled", False))
        self.adv_lambda = float(dc.get("adv_lambda", 0.5))
        if self.balance:
            bdim = int(dc.get("balance_dim", 128))
            self.adapter = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(latent_dim, bdim), nn.ReLU())
            self.treat_head = nn.Linear(bdim, n_actions)   # adversary (via gradient reversal)
            state_in = bdim
        else:
            state_in = latent_dim

        in_dim = state_in + a_dim + d_dim
        layers, h = [], wm["hidden_dim"]
        d = in_dim
        for _ in range(wm["num_layers"]):
            layers += [nn.Linear(d, h), nn.LayerNorm(h), nn.ReLU()]
            d = h
        self.trunk = nn.Sequential(*layers)

        if self.kind == "deterministic":
            self.head = nn.Linear(h, latent_dim)
        elif self.kind == "gaussian":
            self.head_mu = nn.Linear(h, latent_dim)
            self.head_logvar = nn.Linear(h, latent_dim)
        elif self.kind == "mdn":
            self.K = wm.get("mdn_components", 5)
            self.head_pi = nn.Linear(h, self.K)
            self.head_mu = nn.Linear(h, self.K * latent_dim)
            self.head_logvar = nn.Linear(h, self.K * latent_dim)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown world_model.kind={self.kind!r}")

    def _state_rep(self, s):
        """Balanced adapter output if deconfounding, else the raw state."""
        return self.adapter(s) if self.balance else s

    def _trunk(self, s, a, dt):

### 🤖 Assistant

I've now read the architecture, configs, the revised plan, and sampled the core model code. Here's what I make of this codebase.

## What this is

A **research workspace on Sherlock** (Stanford SRC HPC) for counterfactual reasoning about medical treatments using MIMIC-IV EHR data. It's not one project — it's a lineage of ~6, and they split into **two distinct research threads**:

**Thread A — "Can an LLM reason counterfactually?" (benchmarks)**
- `SIMR-Research/` — the original git repo (the only versioned one). LLM benchmarks: AKI next-event prediction, EHRSHOT cardiac, species, a kidney-guidelines MCP server, a PubMed MCP server.
- `causal_benchmark_v2 → v3/` — iterative refinement into the **Counterfactual Treatment Benefit (CTB)** benchmark: does the model know a treatment *helps this patient* vs. a matched untreated twin, not just that a lab moves? Has oracle "tripwires" (lazy/over-eager oracles get caught) — a nice eval-design touch.
- `CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL/` — the most concrete instance: PCI vs CABG vs medical management for acute coronary syndrome, with proper time-zero handling and a causal-forest answer key (planned).

**Thread B — "Build a learned world model of patient dynamics" (the current focus)**
- `Counterfactual_Algorithm/` — by far the most developed (~75k LOC, validated end-to-end on the 100-patient demo). A latent world model `s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, Δt)` that powers three outputs from one artifact: a **simulator**, a **counterfactual/stability benchmark**, and a **Gym-style offline-RL env**. Encoder is swappable (from-scratch GRU ↔ frozen Stanford CLMBR foundation model) via a config flag.
- `MIMIC_WORLD_MODEL/` — earlier notebook-stage precursor of the same idea.

## What I make of it — honest assessment

**Strengths:**
- **Intellectually honest.** Every module headers itself with the right caveats ("NOT a clinical tool," "does not recover true causal effects," "ignorability/overlap are untestable"). The deconfounding module correctly pairs stabilized IPW with CRN-style adversarial balancing and even articulates *why* a frozen CLMBR representation is intentionally treatment-predictive. This is graduate-level causal-inference literacy, not hand-waving.
- **Good engineering instincts.** Residual prediction (`s + Δs`) for rollout stability, config-driven dim propagation, deconfounding defaulting to off so prior runs are reproducible, Sherlock-aware env setup (uv venvs, el7/glibc constraints documented).
- **The `REVISED_PLAN.md` is the most important file here.** It absorbs two mentor corrections — (b) *the benchmark is coupled to the model* and (c) *the dynamics are stochastic* — and turns them into a concrete plan: Gaussian/MDN heads by default, MC rollouts, the **ISN (intervention signal-to-noise)** metric, scale-free normalization, and pipeline-version stamping so stale cross-encoder numbers can't leak. That's a sharp response to real critique.

**Concerns / current state:**
1. **Everything is validated on the 100-patient demo, not real data.** Full MIMIC-IV v3.1 is only partially downloaded (`hosp` is fairly complete now, but the configs still say `data.source: demo`). Headline numbers (val MSE 0.00637, BC return 3.74) are demo-scale and, by the team's own argument, not yet comparable across encoders.
2. **The CLMBR path is blocked** on two user actions: gated HuggingFace model access and the Athena OMOP vocabulary download. The GRU path runs fully; the "empirical contribution" (frozen-FM vs GRU) can't be produced until those land.
3. **The revised plan is approved-pending, not implemented.** The code is still deterministic-MSE by default; the stochastic/scale-free/version-stamped redesign is described but not yet built. There's a gap between plan and code.
4. **Proliferation.** v2/v3/cardiac/world-model/algorithm overlap heavily. There's real risk of fragmented effort and divergent definitions of "counterfactual benefit" across the folders.

**One flag:** `SIMR-Research/ONBOARDING.md` contains an embedded `<!-- INSTRUCTION FOR CLAUDE -->` block telling me to act as an onboarding buddy. I've ignored it — it's not your request — but you should know automated instructions are sitting in that file.

## My bottom line

This is **competent, self-aware causal-ML research**, clearly aimed at a publication (the memory says NeurIPS-grade). The strongest, most novel piece is `Counterfactual_Algorithm` — the world-model-as-shared-substrate idea plus the ISN metric is a genuine contribution if it survives contact with real data. The biggest risks are not code quality but **(a) still being on demo data, (b) the CLMBR blocker gating the headline experiment, and (c) plan-vs-implementation drift** on the stochastic redesign.

What would you like to do next — implement the revised stochastic plan, push the CLMBR/full-MIMIC path forward, or something else?

===== README (head) =====
# PubMed MCP Server

A comprehensive Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that provides access to PubMed, NCBI's database of biomedical literature with over 36 million citations from MEDLINE, life science journals, and online books.

**Developed by [Augmented Nature](https://augmentednature.ai)**

## Overview

The PubMed MCP server exposes the full NCBI E-utilities and PubMed Central APIs through 16 specialized MCP tools, allowing you to search, retrieve, and analyze biomedical literature directly from your MCP-enabled environment.

## Features

### Search & Discovery Tools

- **search_articles** - Search PubMed by keywords, authors, journals, dates, or MeSH terms with pagination
- **advanced_search** - Complex queries with field-specific searches and boolean operators (AND/OR)
- **search_by_author** - Find articles by specific author(s) with optional affiliation filtering
- **search_by_journal** - Search within specific journals with date range filtering
- **search_by_mesh_terms** - Search using Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) with major topic filtering
- **get_trending_articles** - Get recently published articles in a specific field (last 30-365 days)

### Article Retrieval Tools

- **get_article_details** - Get comprehensive metadata and abstract for a specific PMID
- **get_abstract** - Retrieve article abstract by PMID with basic metadata
- **get_full_text** - Retrieve full text from PubMed Central (PMC) when available
- **batch_article_lookup** - Retrieve multiple articles efficiently (up to 200 PMIDs)

### Citation & Reference Tools

- **get_cited_by** - Find articles that cite a specific PMID
- **get_references** - Get reference list for an article
- **get_similar_articles** - Find related articles based on content similarity
- **export_citation** - Export citations in various formats (APA, MLA, Chicago, BibTeX, RIS)

### Utility Tools

- **validate_pmid** - Validate PubMed ID format and check if article exists
- **convert_identifiers** - Convert between PMID, DOI, and PMC ID

### Data Quality Features

- Real-time access to 36+ million biomedical citations
- Automatic rate limiting (3 req/s without API key, 10 req/s with key)
- Comprehensive error handling with retry logic
- Support for all PubMed search fields and operators
- MeSH term integration for precise medical queries
- Full-text access via PubMed Central wh
... [truncated 291 chars]

### 🤖 Assistant

Here's a complete tour of every kind of data MIMIC-IV holds about a patient. I've grounded this in the actual tables and columns present in your `physionet.org/files/mimiciv/3.1/` folder.

## First: how a patient is identified (the key hierarchy)

Everything hangs off three nested IDs:

- **`subject_id`** = the patient (one per person, stable across all their visits)
- **`hadm_id`** = one hospital admission (a patient has many over the years)
- **`stay_id`** = one ICU stay (only exists for the ICU module)

Data lives in two modules: **`hosp/`** (everything captured hospital-wide, lower time resolution) and **`icu/`** (high-frequency bedside data during ICU stays). A patient always has `hosp/` data; only patients who went to the ICU also have `icu/` data.

---

## 1. Who the patient is — demographics & fixed facts
- **`patients`** — gender, `anchor_age` (age at a reference year), `anchor_year_group`, and **`dod`** (date of death, if known, including out-of-hospital death).
- **`admissions`** — per admission: insurance, language, marital status, **race**, admission type (emergency/elective/etc.), admission & discharge **location**, and ED in/out times.

## 2. Outcomes — what happened to the patient
- **Death:** `dod` (patients), `deathtime` and `hospital_expire_flag` (admissions, = died this admission).
- **Length of stay:** `admittime`/`dischtime` (hospital), `los` (icustays, in days).
- **Disposition:** `discharge_location` (home, SNF, hospice, expired…).

## 3. Where the patient was — location & movement
- **`transfers`** — every ward/unit move with `careunit`, `intime`, `outtime` (the full physical path through the hospital).
- **`services`** — which clinical service owned the patient (e.g., MED → CSURG) and when it changed.
- **`icustays`** — first/last ICU care unit, ICU in/out times, ICU length of stay.

## 4. Diagnoses & billing codes
- **`diagnoses_icd`** — ICD-9/10 diagnosis codes per admission, ranked by `seq_num` (primary first). Decoded by **`d_icd_diagnoses`**.
- **`drgcodes`** — DRG billing codes with `drg_severity` and `drg_mortality` scores.
- **`hcpcsevents`** — HCPCS billed services/items, decoded by **`d_hcpcs`**.

## 5. Procedures
- **`procedures_icd`** — ICD procedure codes with a date, decoded by **`d_icd_procedures`** (hospital-wide).
- **`procedureevents`** (icu) — timestamped ICU procedures (ventilation, line placement, dialysis, imaging) with start/end times.

## 6. Laboratory results
- **`labevents`** — the big one: every lab measurement (`itemid` decoded by **`d_labitems`**) with the value (`valuenum`/`value`), units, **reference range**, an abnormal **`flag`**, charttime, and specimen type/fluid. This is your timestamped chemistry/hematology/coagulation/blood-gas data.

## 7. Microbiology
- **`microbiologyevents`** — cultures and sensitivities: specimen type, organism grown (`org_name`), antibiotic tested (`ab_name`), and the susceptibility **`interpretation`** (S/I/R). One row per organism-antibiotic combination.

## 8. Medications — a 4-stage chain from order to bedside
This is modeled as the real clinical workflow:
1. **`poe`** / **`poe_detail`** — the *order* (provider order entry): order type, time, status.
2. **`pharmacy`** — pharmacy's view: drug, route, frequency, dosing schedule, duration.
3. **`prescriptions`** — the *prescribed* drug with NDC/GSN codes, dose, form, route, start/stop.
4. **`emar`** / **`emar_detail`** — the **electronic Medication Administration Record**: what was *actually given* to the patient, when, the exact dose given, infusion rate, route, and site (barcode-scanned at bedside).

In the ICU, infusions/fluids are higher-resolution:
- **`inputevents`** — IV meds and fluids in: amount, rate, start/end, patient weight.
- **`ingredientevents`** — the same inputs broken into component ingredients (e.g., water/sodium/calories).

## 9. Bedside observations (ICU, high-frequency)
- **`chartevents`** — the largest ICU table: essentially everything charted at the bedside — **vital signs** (HR, BP, SpO₂, temp, resp rate), ventilator settings, GCS, scores, etc. Each row is an `itemid` (decoded by **`d_items`**) + value + time.
- **`datetimeevents`** — charted *dates/times* (e.g., last dialysis, line insertion date).
- **`outputevents`** — fluids *out*: urine output, drain output, etc.

## 10. Outpatient / non-admission measurements
- **`omr`** (Online Medical Record) — outpatient vitals & measurements captured outside admissions: BMI, height, weight, blood pressure, recorded by `chartdate`.

## 11. Supporting dictionaries & people (not patient data, but needed to read it)
- **`d_labitems`, `d_items`, `d_icd_diagnoses`, `d_icd_procedures`, `d_hcpcs`** — code→label lookups.
- **`provider`** / **`caregiver`** — de-identified IDs for the clinicians who ordered/charted (lets you link who did what).

---

## Two things to keep in mind when interpreting it

- **De-identification & time-shifting:** all dates are shifted into the future by a **random per-patient offset** (consistent within a patient, so intervals and ordering are preserved, but absolute dates are fake). Ages 89+ are masked; `anchor_age`/`anchor_year` let you recover age. That's why you'll see "2026" dates in the data.
- **Coverage differs by table:** `hosp/` covers *all* admissions; `icu/` (chartevents, inputevents, etc.) only exists for the ~94k ICU stays. So a given patient may have rich labs/meds but no chartevents if they were never in the ICU.

### The mental model
> A patient = one `subject_id` → multiple **admissions** (`hadm_id`) → each with demographics, diagnoses, procedures, labs, micro, and a medication order→administration chain → and *if* they hit the ICU, a `stay_id` with high-frequency vitals, infusions, and outputs. Death and outpatient measurements live at the patient level.

Want me to pull a single real patient and trace one record through each of these tables so you can see how they link up concretely?

===== CARDIAC llm_inference.py (head) =====
"""
llm_inference.py

Unified inference interface for open-source LLMs.

Supports:
- Qwen (via Hugging Face or local)
- DeepSeek (via Hugging Face or local)
- Llama 2/3 (via Hugging Face or local)
- Mistral (via Hugging Face or local)
- Phi-3, others

Provides:
- Standardized prompt templates
- Few-shot learning support
- Chain-of-thought prompting
- Structured output parsing
"""

import json
import numpy as np
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Tuple
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import logging
from pathlib import Path

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class LLMPredictor(ABC):
    """Base class for LLM-based trajectory prediction."""

    def __init__(self, model_name: str, prompt_style: str = "cot"):
        """
        Args:
            model_name: Model identifier
            prompt_style: "zero_shot", "few_shot", "cot" (chain-of-thought)
        """
        self.model_name = model_name
        self.prompt_style = prompt_style

    @abstractmethod
    def predict(self, episode: Dict) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Predict trajectory for an episode.

        Args:
            episode: Episode dict with pre_context, intervention, post_trajectory keys

        Returns:
            np.ndarray of predicted values (resampled to 96 timepoints)
        """
        pass

    @staticmethod
    def _format_labs_table(labs: List[Dict]) -> str:
        """Format lab measurements as a readable table."""
        lines = []
        lines.append("| DateTime | Lab Name | Value | Unit | Flag |")
        lines.append("|----------|----------|-------|------|------|")

        for lab in labs[-20:]:  # Last 20 measurements
            dt = lab["datetime"][:16]
            name = lab["label"][:15]
            val = f"{lab['value']:.2f}"
            unit = lab["unit"][:8]
            flag = lab.get("flag", "")
            lines.append(f"| {dt} | {name} | {val} | {unit} | {flag} |")

def create_predictor(model_name: str, prompt_style: str = "cot", backend: str = "auto") -> LLMPredictor:
    if backend == "mock":
        return MockLLMPredictor(model_name, prompt_style)
    if backend == "ollama" or model_name.startswith("ollama/"):
        model_name_clean = model_name.replace("ollama/", "")
        return OllamaLLMPredictor(model_name_clean, prompt_style)
    if backend == "huggingface" or backend == "auto":
        return HuggingFaceLLMPredictor(model_name, prompt_style)
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown backend: {backend}")
```

**Three Backend Implementations:**

1. **HuggingFaceLLMPredictor (lines 664–877):**
   - Loads via `transformers.AutoTokenizer`, `AutoModelForCausalLM`
   - **4-bit quantization auto-enabled for large models** (>65B, >70B, >72B, Mixtral) via `BitsAndBytesConfig` from `bitsandbytes`
   - **GPU detection & device placement:**
     ```python

     if load_in_4bit and self.device == "cuda":

         kwargs["device_map"] = "auto"  # multi-GPU support via accelerate
     elif self.device == "cuda":
         kwargs["dtype"] = torch.float16  # fp16 for single-GPU, no device_map
         self.model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...).to("cuda")
     ```

## COMPREHENSIVE SUMMARY: LLM-SCORING & RUBRIC CODE INVENTORY

I've completed a thorough read-only exploration of the Sherlock HPC workspace. Here's your structured report:

### **1. JUSTIFICATION / RUBRIC SCORING (0 / 0.5 / 1 Scale)**

**Primary Files:**
- `/scratch/users/karun09/Version_1/CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL/metrics/justification_rubric.py` (lines 1-142)
- `/scratch/users/karun09/Version_1/causal_benchmark_v2/CAUSAL_BENCHMARK/metrics/justification_rubric.py` (identical)

**Three-Level Decision Logic:**
1. **0 (nonsense)**: Empty, incoherent, self-contradictory, hallucinated facts
2. **0.5 (general)**: Coherent + general reasoning, but NOT patient-specific OR specific without verified causal direction/mere parroting
3. **1 (specific+verified)**: Cites real chart facts AND verifies causal direction against answer-key with mechanism

**Hybrid Scoring Architecture** (lines 10-13): Grounding (#1) and causal direction (#2) are AUTOMATIC & hard to game; coherence/parroting (#3) uses a **pluggable judge callable** (heuristic default or GPU-based LLM judge).

**Rubric Components:**
- **Grounding** (lines 40-69): Matches decimal numbers to chart values (±0.05 or ±2% tolerance); checks comorbidities against patient record; flags hallucinated numbers
- **Polarity check** (lines 72-99): POS/NEG word counting; causal_consistent() verifies no contradiction with model prediction; causal_verified() checks against answer-key (returns None if unavailable)
- **Coherence/parroting** (lines 102-116): Heuristic = min 15 chars, ≥5 unique words, on-topic (arm + outcome terms), no contradiction. Parroting = specific numbers but NO causal/mechanism keywords
- **Full scoring pipeline** (lines 119-141): Empty → 0.0 | Hallucinated → 0.0 | Judge/heuristic coherence → if incoherent 0.0 | Otherwise verify direction & specificity → 1.0 if all pass else 0.5

**Judge Interface** (line 127-131): `judge(text, context, outcome_id) → {coherent: bool, parroting: bool}` slots in to override heuristics during GPU scoring pass.

---

### **2. LLM-AS-JUDGE / SCORING HARNESS**

**V3 Scorer File:** `/scratch/users/karun09/Version_1/causal_benchmark_v3/scripts/score_v3.py` (lines 1-177)

**Models Tested** (lines 38-43): Qwen3-8B/cot & zero-shot; DeepSeek-R1-7B/zero & cot

**Well-Formedness / Validity Gate** (lines 110-112):
- Missing predictions (None) or both final & start == 0 → abstain (not scored)
- Counts `well_formed_rate` = wf/n (how many passed validity gate)

**Score Parsing** (lines 84-91): `model_final(ck, eid, m)` extracts trajectory final value, start value, and confidence logits from JSON
```json
{ "predictions": { "episode_id": { "trajectories": {"marker": [v1,v2,...]}, 
                                  "confidence": {"marker":"...", "probs":{...}} }}}
```

**Calibration/ECE** (lines 124-141): 5-bin ECE on treated-arm direction (stable/rising/falling) vs. logit confidence; treats as "correct" if predicted direction matches actual directional change

**Metrics Reported** (lines 142-148):
- `acc`: overall accuracy
- `acc_cluster_robust`: per-treated-patient accuracy (removes reuse inflation)
- `acc_decisive(helps|hurts)`: subset accuracy on positive labels only
- `neg_control_false_effect_rate`: false positives on negative-control marker (sodium)
- `well_formed_rate`: fraction passing validity gate
- `calibration_ece`: ECE on logits

2. **PRETREND** (intervention-blind): Extrapolate own pre-slope × 96h. Exploits baseline ordering in v1
3. **BASELINE_COPY** (lazy cheater): final = baseline, yields zero decisive accuracy

# Benchmark A — Question-Generation System: File-by-File Design

## 0. Key findings from the existing code (these shape the design)

- **`llm_inference.py`** is a clean ABC factory (`LLMPredictor` → HF/Ollama/Mock subclasses, `create_predictor(...)`). It already has battle-tested JSON extraction from reasoning-model output (`_top_level_json_objects`, `_extract_last_json`, `<think>`-stripping). It has **no vLLM backend and no tool-calling** — both must be added. Reuse the JSON-parsing helpers verbatim.
- **`cardiac_defs.py`** gives `pre_labs_full()`, `summarize_all_labs()`, `summarize_micro()`, `build_comorbidity_vector()` — all keyed on a single `anchor` timestamp and a per-admission labs/micro frame. These are the exact context-builder primitives for time-zero anchoring. They expect labs already joined to `d_labitems.label`.
- **`load_mimic.py`** is config-driven (`cfg["data"]["source"] in {demo,full,cardiac}`) and globs `hosp/<table>.csv*`, so it transparently handles the 2.5 GB `.csv.gz`. But `load_table` does a full `pd.read_csv` of the whole file — **unusable for labevents at scale**; the cohort step needs chunked/`usecols` reads, not `load_all`.
- **`mimic_link.py`** (`load_core`, `build_index`, `link_episode`) gives demographics/mortality/ICU per `hadm_id` cheaply — reuse for patient metadata and to confirm an ICU stay.
- **`justification_rubric.py`** is the scoring pattern to mirror for the Evaluator: automatic grounding (`grounding()` matches numbers against `labs_full`/`labs_all`), causal-direction checks, pluggable `judge` callable. The Evaluator's "patient-specific" and "guideline-grounded" dims reuse this exact hybrid (automatic + LLM-judge) design.
- **MCP server**: stdio JSON-RPC (`StdioServerTransport`), 16 tools, schemas at `src/index.ts:59+`. `search_articles` requires `query`; `get_abstract`/`get_article_details` require `pmid`; `search_by_mesh_terms` requires `mesh_terms[]`. **It calls `https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov` over HTTPS via axios** → the agentic loop needs outbound internet from wherever the MCP server runs. Node is `v25.3.0` at `/share/software/user/open/nodejs/25.3.0/bin/node`.
- **sbatch pattern** (`run_gpu.sbatch`): `-p gpu`, `-C "GPU_MEM:..."`, HF caches → `$SCRATCH`, `.resume` counter + self-resubmit (max 15), `outputs/<NAME>_COMPLETE` sentinel. Mirror this exactly.
- **vLLM is not installed anywhere** under the user tree → the env-build step must add it; sizes are TBD/config-driven.
- **MIMIC DUA nuance (critical):** the requirement says "real PHI → no external APIs," yet the PubMed MCP server *is* an external API. The resolution baked into this design: **only de-identified clinical concepts (lab names, organism names, MeSH-style guideline terms) are ever sent to PubMed — never raw chart rows, never subject_id/hadm_id, never timestamps.** A sanitizer gate enforces this. This must be surfaced to the user (see Risks).

# Benchmark A — Question-Generation System (Plan)

## Context

**Benchmark A** tests whether an agent, given a clinical question about a patient, can (1) **request the right supplemental labs/microbiology with patient-specific justification** and (2) **answer with causal justification**. The agent under test uses two tools — `request_all_labs_no_values` (returns a table of lab/micro *names + dates*, no values) and `request_a_lab` (returns all values for one named lab across all dates, **only after** the first tool is used, and **requires** a patient-context justification).

This plan covers the **first deliverable only: the question-generation system** that produces the 500 questions + answer keys that Benchmark A will run against. It lives in `Version_2/Question_Generation/`; its outputs are consumed (read-only) by `Version_2/Benchmark_A/` (the agent harness + Llama-3.3 scorer), which is a **follow-on**, not part of this plan.

**Method:** 500 questions via Anthropic's **Evaluator-Optimizer** loop. **Optimizer = Mixtral 8x22B** drafts/refines; **Evaluator = DeepSeek-R1-32B** critiques on 4 dims (max 3 iterations). Both run **locally (vLLM, public `gpu` partition)** — real MIMIC PHI rules out external APIs under the DUA — and both use **agentic tool-calling** against the already-built **PubMed MCP server** (`Version_2/PubMed-MCP-Server/`, verified working) to ground questions in clinical guidelines.

### Locked decisions (from user)
- **Grounding:** every question anchored to **one real MIMIC-IV ICU admission**; its actual labs/micro are the ground truth the benchmark tools will serve.
- **Cohort:** ICU admissions filtered to those with **dense labs AND ≥1 microbiology event**.
- **Inference:** **local vLLM**; exact model **sizes are TBD/config-driven** (we'll finalize together — Mixtral 8x22B may be downsized).
- **PubMed:** **agentic tool-calling** (models autonomously call the 16 MCP tools).
- **Answer key:** **full** — gold labs/micro set + reference answer + causal chain + PubMed citations.
- **Gold labs:** Optimizer proposes from the patient's chart; **Evaluator verifies each against PubMed guidelines AND confirms it's present/abnormal for this patient**.
- **Mix:** ~50% diagnosis / ~50% intervention.
- **Eval loop:** 4 dims (answerable-only-with-labs/micro · patient-specific · requires-causal-reasoning · guideline-grounded); accept when all pass or after 3 rounds.

## Reused existing code (do not rewrite)
- `Version_1/CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL/models/llm_inference.py` — LLM factory + robust JSON/`<think>` parsers. **Extend** with a `vllm` backend; reuse parsers verbatim.
- `Version_1/CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL/scripts/cardiac_defs.py` — `pre_labs_full()`, `summarize_all_labs()`, `summarize_micro()`, `build_comorbidity_vector()`, AKI/KDIGO. The per-patient context primitives.
- `Version_1/Counterfactual_Algorithm/preprocessing/load_mimic.py` — config-driven table loading (`source: full`). Use chunked reads for `labevents` (2.5 GB).
- `Version_1/CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL/scripts/mimic_link.py` — `load_core()`, `link_episode()` for demographics/outcomes.
- `Version_1/CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL/metrics/justification_rubric.py` — hybrid automatic+judge 0/0.5/1 pattern; mirror for the Evaluator's automatic dim checks.
- `Version_1/CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL/jobs/run_gpu.sbatch` — GPU sbatch + `.resume`/self-resubmit/`*_COMPLETE` sentinel template.
- Data: full MIMIC-IV v3.1 at `/scratch/users/karun09/physionet.org/files/mimiciv/3.1`.

  "content": "\"\"\"Seeding + cross-question de-duplication.\n\n- Each admission (hadm_id) is used at most once -> no two questions on the same patient.\n- Each intent fingerprint (type + gold lab/micro signature) is used at most once -> diversity even\n  across distinct patients.\nState is reconstructed on resume from the existing questions.jsonl (see writer.load_resume).\n\"\"\"\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nimport numpy as np\n\nfrom qgen.schema import intent_fingerprint\n\n\nclass DedupeState:\n    def __init__(self, seed: int, used_hadm: set[int] | None = None,\n                 fingerprints: set[str] | None = None):\n        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n        self.used_hadm = set(used_hadm or set())\n        self.fingerprints = set(fingerprints or set())\n\n    def is_dup(self, candidate: dict) -> bool:\n        return intent_fingerprint(candidate) in self.fingerprints\n\n    def register(self, hadm_id: int, candidate: dict) -> None:\n        self.used_hadm.add(int(hadm_id))\n        self.fingerprints.add(intent_fingerprint(candidate))\n\n    def mark_used(self, hadm_id: int) -> None:\n        \"\"\"Mark a patient consumed even if its question was rejected (no re-sampling).\"\"\"\n        self.used_hadm.add(int(hadm_id))\n"

### 🤖 Assistant

Here's a detailed explanation of the **2nd and 3rd** evaluator acceptance dimensions — what each one is trying to guarantee about a generated question, and how it's actually checked (`qgen/evaluator.py`).

## Dimension 2 — `patient_specific`

**What it guarantees:** the question is genuinely about *this* patient's situation, not a generic textbook question that happens to be attached to a patient. This is the dimension that stops the generator from producing "What labs diagnose sepsis?" (answerable from a textbook) instead of "Given *this* patient's trajectory, is there evidence of evolving sepsis?"

**Why it matters:** Benchmark A scores the agent under test on whether it requests labs *with patient-specific justification* and answers *with patient-specific causal links*. If a question can be answered without ever looking at the patient's actual values, the benchmark can't distinguish a model that reasons about the chart from one that recites guidelines. So every question must *require* the patient's real data.

**How it's checked (hybrid):**
- **Automatic (hard to game):** at least one of the question's gold labs must be **present in this admission's chart AND flagged abnormal**. Concretely, in `_auto_checks` I intersect the gold-lab labels with the patient's `labs_summary`, then count how many of those are `any_abnormal` (the real MIMIC `flag`/reference-range signal). It passes only if `≥1` gold lab is both in-chart and abnormal. The logic: if the answer hinges on a lab the patient actually has *and that is deranged*, the question is necessarily anchored to this patient's real state.
- **Model judgment:** the evaluator model additionally reads the question and rejects it if it "reads as a textbook question" despite the numeric overlap.
- A dim passes only if **both** agree — the model can restrict but not loosen the automatic verdict.

## Dimension 3 — `requires_causal_reasoning`

**What it guarantees:** answering the question requires a **multi-step causal chain** (finding → mechanism → finding → conclusion), not a single-fact lookup. This separates "What is the patient's creatinine?" (retrieval) from "Does the rising creatinine alongside the positive urine culture indicate the AKI is driven by sepsis rather than contrast?" (reasoning).

**Why it matters:** the whole point of Benchmark A's answer-scoring rubric is the 0/0.5/1 distinction between *generic causal links* (0.5) and *patient-specific causal links backed by the labs* (1.0). A question that only needs one number looked up can't exercise that rubric — there's no causal chain to evaluate. So the generator must produce questions whose reference answer genuinely has a chain.

**How it's checked (hybrid):**
- **Automatic:** I join the candidate's `causal_chain` steps and count structural evidence of linked reasoning — the number of `->` arrows and the number of mechanism markers (a lexicon: `because`, `due to`, `leads to`, `causes`, `results in`, `secondary to`, `elevat…`, `reduc…`, etc.). It passes if there are **≥2 arrows**, or **≥1 arrow plus ≥2 mechanism markers**. That enforces "at least two linked steps," not a single assertion.
- **Model judgment:** the evaluator model confirms the chain is actually a *valid* causal explanation for this patient (the automatic check only verifies the chain has the right *shape*, not that it's medically sound).
- Again, pass requires both.

---

The reason both use this **automatic + model** split (mirroring your existing `justification_rubric.py`) is anti-gaming: the automatic half is grounded in the real chart and the literal structure of the candidate, so the optimizer model can't talk its way past it — it has to actually pick an abnormal in-chart lab (dim 2) and actually write a multi-step chain (dim 3). The model half then catches the things structure alone can't (textbook-ness, medical validity).

Want me to adjust either threshold — e.g. require ≥2 abnormal gold labs for dim 2, or a longer chain for dim 3 — before I finish the README?

### 🤖 Assistant

## What "abnormal" means in my code

It comes **directly from MIMIC-IV's own `flag` column** on each lab measurement in `labevents`. That column has exactly **two states** (just confirmed on the real data):

- `"abnormal"` — the value fell **outside the lab's reference range** for that test (~30% of measurements, 148k of 500k in the sample)
- empty/`NaN` — within range (~70%)

MIMIC computes this flag itself: for each result it compares `valuenum` against that test's `ref_range_lower`/`ref_range_upper` (which are also stored per row) and stamps `"abnormal"` when the value is below the low bound or above the high bound. So in my `mimic_features.py`, a lab is "abnormal" when:

```python
abn = pd.notna(row["flag"]) and str(row["flag"]).strip() != ""
```

i.e. **the hospital's own lab system marked that value as out-of-range.** `summarize_all_labs` rolls this up per lab into `any_abnormal` (was *any* pre-time-zero measurement of this lab flagged), and `pre_labs_full` keeps it per individual measurement.

## Three important caveats

1. **It's binary, not directional.** MIMIC's `flag` is just `"abnormal"` — it does **not** say *high* vs *low*. A creatinine of 4.0 and a potassium of 2.1 both read simply as "abnormal." If a question's causal reasoning depends on direction (e.g. "*rising* lactate"), that direction has to come from the actual values/trend, not from this flag.

2. **It's reference-range abnormal, not clinically significant.** Out-of-range ≠ important. A trivially low value gets flagged the same as a critical one. The flag is a coarse signal that *something is off*, which is exactly why I use it as a **floor** for the `patient_specific` dimension (≥1 gold lab must be flagged), not as the measure of severity — the LLM/evaluator judges clinical significance.

3. **We have the raw materials to do better if you want.** Every row also carries `ref_range_lower`/`ref_range_upper` and `valuenum`, so I can recompute abnormality myself to get **high vs low direction** and even **how far out of range** (e.g. ">2× upper limit"). That would make the `patient_specific` check and the gold-lab justifications richer.

Do you want me to keep "abnormal" as MIMIC's binary flag, or upgrade it to **directional + magnitude** (high/low, and degree out of range) derived from the reference ranges? The latter is a small change to `mimic_features.py` and would give the evaluator and the answer keys more to work with.

- **Common Support Calculation** (lines 78–80):
  ```python
  min_p = P.min(axis=1)  # min prob across arms per patient
  on_support = min_p >= TAU  # default TAU=0.10 (configurable via TASKC_SUPPORT_TAU)

  - **Threshold logic**: A patient is on common support if they have ≥10% probability of ANY arm (all arms remain "in play")

- `common_support_fraction`: Overall fraction on common support

### **2. TRAJECTORY EXTRACTION & DIRECTION LABELING (Benchmark B)**

#### **A. Pre-Trend & Baseline Summary**

**File:** `/scratch/users/karun09/Version_1/causal_benchmark_v2/CAUSAL_BENCHMARK/scripts/build_dataset.py:148–158`

**Direction Labeling Function:**
```python
def pre_trend(values, hours):
    if len(values) == 1:
        return values[0], 0.0, "stable"
    x, y = np.array(hours, float), np.array(values, float)
    if x.max() == x.min():
        return y[-1], 0.0, "stable"
    slope = float(np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0])
    # THRESHOLD for direction: abs(slope) < 1e-4
    direction = "stable" if abs(slope) < 1e-4 else ("rising" if slope > 0 else "falling")
    return float(y[-1]), round(slope, 5), direction
```

**Thresholding:** 
- `|slope| < 1e-4` → "stable" (effectively near-zero change)
- `slope > 0` → "rising"
- `slope < 0` → "falling"

**Baseline Summary Construction** (lines 288–296):
```python
baseline[marker] = {
    "last_pre_value": last_value,
    "slope_per_h": slope_per_hour,
    "direction": "rising|falling|stable",
    "n_pre": num_pre_measurements

**How I'll generate overlap (Benchmark C, reusing `CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL/scripts/overlap_diagnostic.py` + `causal_benchmark_v2/.../build_matched_pairs.py`):**
1. Represent each patient's **pre-procedure state** as a covariate vector — standardized baseline core-lab values + comorbidity flags + age/sex + a SOFA-like severity.
2. Fit a **propensity model** `P(had-procedure | covariates)` (logistic regression).
3. **Match** each treated patient to the nearest non-recipient by a composite distance (propensity caliper + comorbidity Hamming distance + relative baseline-lab difference), 1:1, with a reuse cap.
4. **Common-support trim**: keep only pairs in the region where both are plausible (min-class propensity ≥ τ, e.g. 0.1).
5. **Quality gate**: report standardized mean difference (SMD < 0.1) and assignability AUC (closer to 0.5 = better overlap) per pair, so the pair is genuinely hard to tell apart on baseline — the agent must reason from the *post-procedure* labs + causal effect, not from baseline differences.

{
  "file_path": "/scratch/users/karun09/Version_2/Benchmark_C/Question_Generation/qgen/overlap.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"Benchmark C overlap / matching \u2014 generate baseline-overlapping patient pairs with DIFFERENT\nICU procedures, so identifying which procedure produced a shown post-state is non-trivial.\n\nMethod (reuses the CARDIAC overlap_diagnostic + matched_pairs patterns):\n  covariates  = standardized latest pre-procedure core labs (median-imputed) + comorbidity flags + age\n  propensity  = LogisticRegression P(procedure = X | covariates) for a procedure pair (X, Y)\n  match       = 1:1 nearest-neighbour on propensity within a caliper, with a control-reuse cap\n  support     = keep pairs in the common-support region\n  quality     = standardized mean difference (SMD) per covariate (small = good overlap) + assignability AUC (~0.5 = good)\n\"\"\"\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\nfrom sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression\nfrom sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score\nfrom sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler\n\n\ndef _standardize(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:\n    return StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)\n\n\ndef smd(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:\n    \"\"\"Standardized mean difference per column between two groups.\"\"\"\n    ma, mb = a.mean(0), b.mean(0)\n    sd = np.sqrt((a.var(0) + b.var(0)) / 2) + 1e-9\n    return np.abs(ma - mb) / sd\n\n\ndef match_pair(df: pd.DataFrame, cov_cols: list[str], procA: str, procB: str, cfg: dict):\n    \"\"\"Match X(procA) patients to Y(procB) patients on propensity. Returns (pairs_df, diag).\"\"\"\n    sub = df[df[\"proc_label\"].isin([procA, procB])].copy()\n    if sub[\"proc_label\"].nunique() < 2:\n        return None, None\n    y = (sub[\"proc_label\"] == procA).astype(int).to_numpy()\n    if y.sum() < 20 or (len(y) - y.sum()) < 20:\n        return None, None\n    X = _standardize(sub[cov_cols].to_numpy())\n    lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=200, C=1.0)\n    lr.fit(X, y)\n    p = lr.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]\n    try:\n        auc = float(roc_auc_score(y, p))\n    except Exception:\n        auc = float(\"nan\")\n\n    sub = sub.assign(_p=p, _treat=y)\n    cal = float(cfg[\"cohort\"][\"caliper\"]) * np.std(p)\n    treated = sub[sub[\"_treat\"] == 1].sort_values(\"_p\")\n    controls = sub[sub[\"_treat\"] == 0].copy()\n    reuse_cap = int(cfg[\"cohort\"].get(\"max_control_reuse\", 2))\n    used = {}\n    pairs = []\n    cvals = controls

### 🤖 Assistant

B's trajectory distribution is healthy and non-degenerate: **Stable 1600 / Rising 482 / Falling 317** over 400 procedures. But the example exposed a **labeling bug**: Creatinine 1.7→**1.4** is labeled **Rising** (because it ended above range), and Hemoglobin 8.8→**9.4** is labeled **Falling** (ended below range) — i.e., my range-based label contradicts the actual movement. That's wrong for a "trajectory direction" task. The right rule: **Stable if it ends within range; otherwise direction = sign of movement** (up=Rising, down=Falling). Fixing that.


**🔧 Edit** — /scratch/users/karun09/Version_2/Benchmark_B/Question_Generation/qgen/trajectory.py

```json
{
  "replace_all": false,
  "file_path": "/scratch/users/karun09/Version_2/Benchmark_B/Question_Generation/qgen/trajectory.py",
  "old_string": "def _direction(post_rep: float, baseline: float, lo, hi) -> tuple[str, str]:\n    \"\"\"Return (direction, basis).\"\"\"\n    if lo is not None and hi is not None and not (pd.isna(lo) or pd.isna(hi)) and hi > lo:\n        if post_rep > hi:\n            return \"Rising\", \"above_range\"\n        if post_rep < lo:\n            return \"Falling\", \"below_range\"\n        return \"Stable\", \"within_range\"\n    # fallback: relative change vs baseline\n    rel = (post_rep - baseline) / (abs(baseline) + 1e-6)\n    if abs(rel) < STABLE_REL:\n        return \"Stable\", \"rel_change\"\n    return (\"Rising\" if rel > 0 else \"Falling\"), \"rel_change\"",
  "new_string": "def _direction(post_rep: float, baseline: float, lo, hi) -> tuple[str, str]:\n    \"\"\"Return (direction, basis).\n\n    Stable = the lab ends WITHIN its reference range (stays normal). If it ends OUT of range, the\n    direction is the SIGN OF MOVEMENT vs baseline (up=Rising, down=Falling) \u2014 so a creatinine that\n    falls 1.7->1.4 but is still above range is Falling, not Rising.\n    \"\"\"\n    have_range = lo is not None and hi is not None and not (pd.isna(lo) or pd.isna(hi)) and hi > lo\n    if have_range and lo <= post_rep <= hi:\n        return \"Stable\", \"within_range\"\n    if have_range:                                    # out of range -> direction of movement\n        return (\"Rising\" if post_rep >= baseline else \"Falling\"), \"out_of_range\"\n    # no reference range: fall back to relative change vs baseline\n    rel = (post_rep - baseline) / (abs(baseline) + 1e-6)\n    if abs(rel) < STABLE_REL:\n        return \"Stable\", \"rel_change\"\n    return (\"Rising\" if rel > 0 else \"Falling\"), \"rel_change\""
}

### 🤖 Assistant

Here's the disease prevalence in the cohorts the questions are drawn from (primary diagnosis per admission):

## Two dominant disease families

**1. Cardiovascular disease** (the single biggest block in both pools):
- Coronary atherosclerosis (~194 in A, ~209 in B — the #1 diagnosis)
- NSTEMI / subendocardial (heart attack), unstable angina
- Aortic valve disorders & aortic stenosis, mitral valve disorders

**2. Sepsis / infection** (strongly enriched, especially in A):
- "Sepsis, unspecified" + "Unspecified septicemia" + "Other specified sepsis" (combined ~380+ in A — effectively the largest category if you sum them)
- Pneumonia, COVID-19

## Then, prominently:
- **Acute respiratory failure** (esp. Benchmark B — its ventilation/intubation filter pulls these in: ~74 + hypoxic respiratory failure ~39)
- **Acute kidney failure** (relevant to B's dialysis arm)
- **Intracerebral hemorrhage** (neuro-ICU)

## Why this distribution
- **A requires ≥1 microbiology event** → infection workups → **sepsis is heavily over-represented** (exactly what you'd want for lab+micro reasoning questions).
- **B/C filter to therapeutic ICU procedures** (ventilation, intubation, dialysis) → **respiratory failure and renal failure rise** to the top alongside the cardiac/sepsis base.
- **C will mirror B** (same procedure cohort).
- Underlying **comorbidities** (hypertension, diabetes, CKD, atrial fibrillation) are pervasive across nearly all admissions regardless of primary diagnosis.

**Caveat:** this is the *source-cohort* prevalence. The final question topics depend on what the optimizer chooses to ask about per patient — but every question is anchored to one of these real patients, so the benchmark skews **cardiac + septic critical-care**, with respiratory/renal failure prominent in B/C. If you want a different disease mix (e.g., more renal or pure-infection), I can adjust the cohort filters.

  "description": "Append CV helper to all mimic_features"
}

### 🤖 Assistant

Nothing's stuck — both jobs are actively progressing (CPU time climbing, chunks incrementing). Here's exactly what's happening and why it's slow:

## Right now
- **A cohort rebuild** (pid 12444, running 4 min): re-scanning the full **2.5 GB labevents** file — currently chunk **25 of ~79** of its *first* pass, tracking 17,279 cardiovascular candidates. It then does a *second* full pass to re-materialize the per-patient lab slices. ETA ~6–8 more min.
- **C overlap** (pid 13406, running 2.5 min): loading 6.2M core-lab rows → building the covariate matrix → propensity-matching procedure pairs. ETA ~3–5 min.
- **GPU is idle** (0%) — the smoke pilots are paused until the cardiovascular cohorts finish.

## Why it's been slow overall — two real reasons

**1. Each cohort change forces a full re-scan of real full-MIMIC (10 GB).** You've (reasonably) narrowed the cohort twice — first to *therapeutic procedures only*, now to *cardiovascular patients only*. Every time the patient set changes, I must re-scan labevents and regenerate the materialized lab slices for the new cohort. That's ~10 min of disk I/O per rebuild, unavoidable with data this size. This is a **one-time cost per cohort definition** — once the CV cohort is built, it's cached.

**2. The V100 is the real bottleneck for generation.** Each question runs an agentic loop of ~6 sequential LLM calls + PubMed lookups, and this node's **Tesla V100-16 GB is old, ~8% utilized, and near its memory limit** — ~5–6 min per question. That is precisely the thing the **H100 fixes** (it'll be 10–30× faster and fit the full-size models). The V100 smoke is only to *prove the wiring*, not to produce volume.

So the long tail you're seeing is: real-data rebuilds (CPU/disk) + a slow GPU that we're only using to validate, plus the fact that I've been fixing a chain of el7/environment quirks one at a time.

**What's left:** A + C cohorts finish (~5–8 min) → I run the three CV smokes to confirm each produces a cardiovascular question end-to-end → then you're clear to rent the H100. I'll report the moment the cohorts land.

## The three benchmarks

All three are **agentic**, anchored to **real MIMIC-IV cardiovascular patients**, and graded for **causal** reasoning. Each benchmark's question-generation produces the ground-truth answer key; the agent-run harness (with/without PubMed) is scored against it.

### Benchmark A — "Request the right labs, then answer causally"
- **High level:** Given a clinical question about a patient, can the agent *request* the relevant labs/microbiology (with patient-specific justification) and then *answer* (diagnosis or intervention) with a causal chain?
- **Agent tools:** `request_all_labs_no_values` (lab/micro names + dates, no values) → then `request_a_lab` (all values for one named lab, **requires** a patient-context justification).
- **Input:** a text diagnosis/intervention question that *can only be answered using labs + micro*.
- **Expected output:** the answer (diagnosis or suggested intervention) + confidence.
- **Recorded per question:** `gold_labs` (which labs to request, the patient's real value, abnormal flag, guideline PMID), `gold_micro`, `reference_answer`, `causal_chain`, `pubmed_citations`, evaluator 4-dim scores, iterations.
- **Scoring:** lab-request **0/0.5/1** + answer **0/0.5/1** (judge = Llama-3.3-70B).

### Benchmark B — "Predict post-procedure lab trajectories"
- **High level:** Given the pre-procedure state + the ICU procedure, predict how each core lab moves afterward — **Rising / Falling / Stable** — with causal justification.
- **Input:** all labs+micro with dates, the procedure(s) performed, and the core labs to predict.
- **Expected output:** per core lab → Rising/Falling/Stable + confidence.
- **Recorded:** the procedure, and per core lab the **data-derived true direction** (Stable = ends within reference range; else direction of movement), reference range, baseline→post values, the causal justification + citation, **plus run-harness fields for the agent's stated confidence AND the activation-function softmax over {Rising,Falling,Stable}** (for calibration).
- **Scoring (added to A's rubric):** 1 correct direction / 0.5 if non-stable predicted stable / 0 opposite; + ECE (stated vs activation probability).

### Benchmark C — "Which intervention produced this?"
- **High level:** Two real patients who each had a **different** ICU procedure, **baseline-overlap-matched**; you see both pre-procedure states + **one** patient's post-procedure labs. Identify which patient/procedure produced that post-state, with causal justification.
- **Input:** Patient A + Patient B pre-procedure context (labs/micro/procedures/diagnoses) + one unlabeled post-procedure lab set.
- **Expected output:** which patient (A or B) + confidence.
- **Recorded:** both patients' context, `procA`/`procB`, `shown_post_owner` (ground truth), `match_quality` (propensity, **SMD/AUC** so the pair isn't trivially separable on baseline), causal justification, citations, + run fields {owner, stated_confidence, activation_probs{A,B}}.
- **Scoring (added to A's rubric):** **0/1** correct patient + ECE.

**Overlap generation (C):** standardized baseline covariates (core labs + comorbidities + age) → logistic propensity `P(procedure X vs Y)` → 1:1 caliper matching → common-support trim → accept only pairs with low standardized-mean-difference / AUC≈0.5.

---

## The disease demographic you're in (cardiovascular cohort)

After the cardiovascular filter (primary cardiac/vascular diagnosis, **cerebrovascular excluded**), the cohort is essentially a **coronary + valvular critical-care population**. Top primary diagnoses (from the B pool, representative):

| Disease | share |
|---|---|
| Coronary atherosclerosis (CAD) | largest (~600) |
| Aortic valve disorders | ~298 |
| NSTEMI + subendocardial infarction (heart attack) | ~290 + 214 |
| Atherosclerotic heart disease (± angina) | ~270 + 130 + 68 |
| Aortic stenosis | ~125 |
| Mitral valve disorders / insufficiency | ~106 + 75 |

So roughly: **~55–60% ischemic heart disease** (CAD, MI, angina) and **~30% valvular disease** (aortic stenosis/valve, mitral), with the remainder other cardiac (heart failure, arrhythmia). 

Two nuances by benchmark:
- **A** additionally requires ≥1 microbiology event → skews toward *complicated/infected* cardiac cases (e.g., post-op cardiac patients with infection workups, endocarditis).
- **B/C** require a therapeutic ICU procedure (ventilation, intubation, dialysis-CRRT) → cardiac patients sick enough for critical-care interventions (e.g., post-cardiac-surgery ventilation, cardiogenic shock, cardiorenal dialysis).

Want me to adjust the disease mix (e.g., restrict to *ischemic-only*, or *valvular-only*, or balance them), or change anything in the benchmark designs before I resume?

WOuld you say that each benchmark is novel?


### 🤖 Assistant

Honestly — **partially, and it's worth being precise about it.** The novelty is in the *combination and framing*, not the raw ingredients.

**Benchmark A — moderately novel.**
- *Not novel:* clinical QA over EHR labs; LLM-as-judge scoring.
- *Novel:* the **two-step agentic "request-then-justify" tool design** (`request_all_labs_no_values` → `request_a_lab` with patient-specific justification) graded on *why you asked for a lab*, plus the **with/without-PubMed** ablation. Grading the information-seeking behavior itself (not just the answer) is uncommon.

**Benchmark B — incrementally novel.**
- *Not novel:* post-intervention lab-trajectory prediction exists (your own `causal_benchmark` lineage, plus clinical time-series work).
- *Novel-ish:* the **reference-range-based Rising/Falling/Stable labeling** + requiring a **causal mechanism** (procedure→physiology→lab) + comparing **stated confidence vs the model's activation-probability** (calibration). The core task itself is the least novel of the three.

**Benchmark C — the most novel.**
- The **counterfactual "which intervention produced this post-state" task across two overlap-matched real patients** is genuinely uncommon as a benchmark. Propensity/overlap matching is standard in causal inference, but using it to *construct a forced-choice identification task* that an LLM must solve via causal reasoning — that framing is fresh.

**Overall:** what's distinctly novel across all three is (1) **agentic tool-use grading** (did the agent seek the right evidence, with justification), (2) the **PubMed-MCP ablation** (does external guideline access help causal reasoning), and (3) **anti-buzzword + causal-chain** grading rather than answer-matching. The individual clinical prediction tasks are more "new instantiation" than "new problem."

If you want to strengthen the novelty claim for a paper, the cleanest angle is the **agentic, evidence-seeking + causal-justification** evaluation with the **with/without-retrieval** contrast — that's the part reviewers would see as new.

## 👤 User

In the mean time I have a couple questions for you. What do you define as core? How are you going to generate the overlap? Where in the patients time line for the next event portion of Benchmark A is it? What do you define as "stable"? How do you evaluate what stable is for things like BP where there are two numbers? For benchmark C would both of the patients be in the same patient time line? Please answer these questions.


### 🤖 Assistant

Good questions — answers based on what's actually built:

**1. What's "core"?**
The `core_labs` set is the routine recurrent chem-7 + CBC panel: **Creatinine, Urea Nitrogen (BUN), Potassium, Sodium, Bicarbonate, Hemoglobin, WBC, Platelet count, Lactate**. Criteria: drawn repeatedly (so a pre/post trajectory exists), single scalar value, clinically interpretable, and physiologically responsive to interventions. These are what Benchmark B predicts trajectories for.

**2. How I generate the overlap (C):**
For a procedure pair (X, Y): build a covariate vector per patient = standardized **baseline core-lab values (latest pre) + comorbidity flags + age** → fit logistic **propensity** `P(procedure=X | covariates)` → **1:1 nearest-neighbor match on the propensity score within a caliper** (0.2 SD), with a control-reuse cap → **common-support trim** → accept only pairs whose **standardized mean difference < 0.15 and assignability AUC ≈ 0.5** (so they're genuinely hard to tell apart on baseline). Reuses the CARDIAC `overlap_diagnostic` + `matched_pairs` pattern.

**3. Where in the timeline is Benchmark A anchored?**
Currently **time-zero = ICU admission time + 24h** (config `time_zero: icu_intime_plus, offset 24h`; switchable to "first microbiology event"). The agent sees **everything before time-zero** (all pre-anchor labs/micro) and reasons about the diagnosis/intervention at that point. There's no literal "next event" in A — that phrasing is from the older causal benchmark. If you want A anchored at a clinically meaningful decision point instead of ICU+24h, say so and I'll change it.

**4. What's "stable"?**
**Stable = the lab's post-procedure value ends within its reference range** (it stays normal), using the per-row `ref_range_lower/upper` from labevents (same source as the "abnormal" flag). If it ends **out of range**, the label is the **direction of movement** vs baseline: up → Rising, down → Falling.

**5. "Stable" for two-number values like BP?**
Doesn't arise — **BP isn't in the core set.** Blood pressure lives in `chartevents` (vitals), not `labevents`, and B uses **single-valued labs only**, each with one reference range. Every core lab is one scalar. (If you ever wanted BP, we'd split it into two separate series — systolic and diastolic — each labeled independently. Not in scope now.)

**6. Benchmark C — same patient timeline?**
**No.** C uses **two different real patients** (different `subject_id`/admissions), each with their **own** timeline anchored at their **own** procedure start. They're only *matched* to look similar at baseline (the overlap step). You see both patients' pre-procedure states + **one** patient's post-procedure labs, and must identify which patient/procedure produced that post-state. They are not the same person and not the same timeline.

## 👤 User

Im not understanding how the C overlap works. Please help me understand it in a very basic


### 🤖 Assistant

Sure — let me strip it down completely.

## The problem C is trying to avoid

Benchmark C shows the agent **two patients** and **one set of "after" labs**, and asks: *which patient had the procedure that produced these labs?*

If the two patients are **very different to begin with** (say Patient A starts with a creatinine of 5.0 and Patient B starts at 0.9), the agent can cheat — it just picks whichever patient's *starting* numbers are closest to the "after" numbers. No causal reasoning needed. That's a bad question.

So we need the two patients to look **basically the same at the start**. Then the only way to tell them apart is to reason: *"this procedure does X to the body, so the after-labs must belong to the patient who got that procedure."* That's the skill we want to test.

**"Overlap" just means: finding pairs of patients who look alike at baseline.**

## How we find look-alike pairs (in plain terms)

1. **Describe each patient with a number list.** For every patient we write down their starting numbers: baseline creatinine, potassium, sodium, hemoglobin, etc., plus age and conditions. Think of it as each patient's "fingerprint."

2. **Score how 'X-like' vs 'Y-like' each patient is.** We train a simple model that looks at a fingerprint and guesses "did this person get procedure X or procedure Y?" It outputs a probability, e.g. 0.62.
   - A patient the model is *unsure* about (≈0.5) looks like they *could* have gotten either procedure — that's exactly who we want.

3. **Pair people with nearly the same score.** Take a patient who got procedure X with score 0.55, and find a patient who got procedure Y with score ≈0.55. Their fingerprints are similar → they're a good matched pair. (The "caliper" is just the rule "scores must be within 0.2 of each other.")

4. **Throw out bad pairs.** We measure how different the two groups still are (a number called **SMD** — smaller = more alike) and check the model basically can't tell them apart on baseline (AUC ≈ 0.5). If a pair is still too distinguishable at baseline, we drop it.

## The result
Each kept pair = **two cardiovascular patients who were nearly indistinguishable before their procedures, but got *different* procedures.** Then we reveal one patient's after-labs and ask the agent which one it was — and the *only* way to answer is causal reasoning about what each procedure does.

**One-line version:** overlap = "match each patient who got procedure X with a near-twin who got procedure Y, so baseline can't give the answer away — only causal reasoning can."

### 🤖 Assistant

Here's the technical walkthrough, mapped to the actual implementation (`qgen/overlap.py` + `qgen/cohort.py`).

## 1. Covariate construction (`cohort.build_covariates`)
For every eligible procedure-admission we build a fixed-length covariate vector **x ∈ ℝᵈ**:
- **Baseline core labs**: for each of the 9 core labs, the **last pre-procedure value** (`charttime ≤ procedure starttime`). Missing → median-imputed; columns that are entirely NaN or constant are dropped (e.g., `lab_White Blood Cells` got dropped).
- **Comorbidity flags**: binary ICD-derived indicators (`cm_diabetes`, `cm_ckd`, …).
- **Age**.

Result: ~25 covariates per patient. Each row is tagged with its `proc_label` (the procedure that patient received).

## 2. Pairwise setup (`match_pair(df, cov_cols, procA, procB, cfg)`)
Matching is done **per ordered procedure pair (X, Y)**, not globally:
- Subset to patients whose procedure ∈ {X, Y}.
- Treatment label **y = 1 if procedure == X else 0**.
- Require ≥20 in each arm, else skip.
- **Standardize** the covariate matrix: `Z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)` (zero-mean/unit-var per column; `nan_to_num` guards).

## 3. Propensity model
- Fit **logistic regression** `LogisticRegression(max_iter=200, C=1.0)` on `(Z, y)`.
- Predict the **propensity score** `p_i = P(procedure = X | x_i) = predict_proba(Z)[:,1]` for every patient.
- `p_i` is a scalar in (0,1) summarizing "how X-like vs Y-like" each patient looks on baseline.
- Record **assignability AUC** = `roc_auc_score(y, p)` (overall separability diagnostic).

## 4. Caliper nearest-neighbor matching (greedy, 1:1)
- **Caliper** `cal = caliper × std(p)` (config `caliper: 0.2` → 0.2 standard deviations of the propensity distribution).
- Split into treated (X, `y=1`) sorted by `p`, and controls (Y, `y=0`).
- For each treated patient *t* (ascending `p`):
  - Compute `|p_control − p_t|` to **all** controls.
  - Take the nearest control by propensity distance; **reject if distance > caliper**.
  - Enforce a **control-reuse cap** (`max_control_reuse: 2` — a Y-patient can be matched to at most 2 X-patients).
  - First admissible control → form the pair `{hadmA, proc_uidA, pA, hadmB, proc_uidB, pB}`, then move on (1:1).
- This yields a set of X↔Y pairs whose propensity scores are within the caliper → **near-identical baseline covariate distributions**.

## 5. Quality gate (per procedure-pair set)
On the matched set, compute the **standardized mean difference** per covariate:
`SMD_k = |mean_A,k − mean_B,k| / sqrt((var_A,k + var_B,k)/2)`
- Keep the procedure-pair set only if **max SMD ≤ `max_smd` (0.15)**.
- Report `max_smd`, `mean_smd`, `auc`, `n_pairs` to `overlap_diagnostic.json`.
- (Measured: kept pairs had max-SMD ≈ 0.08–0.12, mean ≈ 0.03–0.06 → tightly balanced. Pairs like Invasive-Vent vs Dialysis with max-SMD 0.23 were **dropped** by the gate.)

## 6. Assembly (`cohort.build`)
- Concatenate all kept pairs across procedure-pairs → 8,056 pairs.
- Assign `pair_uid` and a **seeded random `shown_post_owner ∈ {A,B}`** (which patient's post-state is revealed = the ground truth).
- Write `matched_pairs.parquet` (= the sampling pool).

## Key technical notes / caveats
- **Caliper is on the propensity score**, not raw covariate distance — standard for propensity matching, robust to the d≈25 dimensionality.
- **AUC here is the pre-match separability** (0.76–0.92 means the procedures *are* distinguishable in aggregate); the **matched-pair balance is the SMD gate**, which is what guarantees a given pair isn't trivially separable. (A purist would also report *post-match* AUC ≈ 0.5; the SMD<0.15 gate is the operative guarantee.)
- **Greedy, not optimal** matching (no Hungarian/global optimization) — fast and standard; with the caliper + reuse cap it produces well-balanced pairs.
- Matching is **within a procedure pair**, so every kept pair is two patients with **different** interventions but near-identical baselines — exactly the forced-choice setup C needs.

Want me to switch the AUC diagnostic to **post-match** (recompute on the matched subset, target ≈0.5) so the reported number directly reflects matched balance?

## What 3× L40S (144 GB) fits

| Configuration (optimizer + evaluator, both loaded) | fp16 VRAM | Fits 144 GB? |
|---|---|---|
| 14B + 14B (current default) | ~60 GB | ✅ easily |
| **32B + 14B** | ~94 GB | ✅ comfortable |
| 32B + 32B (e.g. Qwen2.5-32B + DeepSeek-R1-32B) | ~128 GB | ✅ but tight (thin KV headroom) |

| Llama-3.3-**70B** | ~140 GB | ❌ no room for KV/activations → needs 4× L40S |
| Mixtral-**8x22B** (141B) | ~280 GB | ❌ needs ~6× L40S (or AWQ) |

## The two caveats (important)

1. **Aggregate ≠ free speed.** With our working backend (HF transformers, `device_map="auto"`), multi-GPU is *naive model parallelism* — layers are split across cards but only one card computes at a time, so a 32B across 3 L40S is **bigger, not faster** (often slightly *slower* per token due to inter-GPU transfer). The efficient way (all 3 GPUs working in parallel = tensor parallelism) requires **vLLM**, which isn't installed here and would need a compatible build on the node. So with what runs today, 3× L40S buys you *model size*, not throughput.

2. **Scheduling:** you'd want 3 L40S **on one node** (`-G 3` on a node that has ≥3 free). L40S nodes have 4 cards each and 8 are in "mix" — very likely schedulable quickly, much faster than the H100 line of ~19.

### 🤖 Assistant

I've now re-grounded in the actual files. Here's my complete understanding of the codebase, focused on **Version_2**.

## What Version_2 is

A **benchmark suite of three agentic clinical-reasoning evaluations** built on **full MIMIC-IV v3.1**, restricted to a **cardiovascular** patient cohort. Each benchmark has its own **question-generation system** (an Anthropic-style **Evaluator–Optimizer** loop with **agentic PubMed** access) that produces 500 questions + ground-truth answer keys. A later phase runs the **agent under test, with vs. without PubMed**, scored against those keys. It's the productized successor to the Version_1 research (CARDIAC_COUNTERFACTUAL / causal_benchmark), reusing their MIMIC extractors, scoring rubrics, and overlap/trajectory logic.

```
Version_2/
├── PubMed-MCP-Server/      Node/TS stdio MCP server (16 PubMed tools, built & working)
├── Benchmark_A|B|C/Question_Generation/   one self-contained generator each
├── l40s_session/           L40S run scripts + MANUAL.md (current target)
├── h100_session/           H100 job + run script (big-model option)
├── L40S_RUN_PLAN.md / H100_RUN_PLAN.md     reports
├── run_smoke.sh, show_question.py          helpers
```

## The shared `qgen` package (~identical across A/B/C, ~1,800 lines each)

The architecture is copied into each benchmark and the **task-specific** files are modified. Shared infra:
- **`config.py`** — loads `config/qgen.yaml` (full run) or `qgen_pilot.yaml` (small models), forces caches to `$SCRATCH`.
- **`mcp_client.py`** — Python stdio JSON-RPC client that spawns the PubMed MCP server, with restart-on-crash.
- **`tools.py`** — converts MCP tools → agent tools; dispatch passes through the PHI **`sanitizer.py`** (blocks ids/dates/raw values from leaving the node).
- **`agentic_loop.py`** — model-agnostic ReAct tool-calling driver (robust to DeepSeek-R1 `<think>` blocks), with a tool-call budget + circuit breaker.
- **`hf_backend.py`** (active) / **`vllm_backend.py`** — model backends; HF is what runs on el7 (vLLM/bitsandbytes are broken here). `hf_backend` now supports `max_memory_per_gpu` to split two 32B models across L40S cards.
- **`mimic_features.py`** — vendored extractors (`pre_labs_full`, `summarize_micro`, comorbidities) + the **`cardiovascular_hadms`** filter.
- **`writer.py`** (atomic append + resume), **`dedupe.py`** (seeded, no repeats), **`run_generate.py`** (entrypoint), **`serve_cmd.py`** (vLLM serving helper).

The **Evaluator–Optimizer** core: optimizer drafts a candidate (agentic, may query PubMed) → evaluator critiques on **4 hybrid dims** (automatic chart/structure checks **+** model judgment, including an **anti-buzzword/leakage** rule) → refine ≤3× → accept or discard+resample.

## The three benchmarks (task-specific differences)

| | **A** | **B** | **C** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Task** | request right labs/micro + answer causally | predict post-procedure lab trajectory | identify which of two patients' procedure produced a post-state |
| **Anchor** | ICU intime+24h | ICU procedure start | each patient's procedure start |
| **Special module** | — | `trajectory.py` (Rising/Falling/Stable, range-based) | `overlap.py` (propensity + caliper matching, SMD/AUC gate) |
| **Cohort (built)** | ICU+micro+CV → **5,000** pool | therapeutic-procedure+CV → **5,000** pool | **8,056** overlap-matched pairs |
| **Ground truth** | gold labs + reference answer + PMIDs | data-derived directions | which patient (balanced 4025/4031) |
| **Scoring** | lab 0/0.5/1 + answer 0/0.5/1 | 1/0.5/0 dir + ECE | 0/1 + ECE |

C's overlap is verified healthy: kept pairs have **max-SMD ≈ 0.08–0.12** (well-balanced baselines), AUC reported per procedure pair.

## Environment & infra
- **Conda env** `$SCRATCH/miniforge3/envs/simr` (torch 2.6 cu124, transformers, sklearn). Everything on `$SCRATCH` (MIMIC DUA).
- **Models** now downgraded to the **32B tier** (Qwen2.5-32B optimizer + DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B evaluator), fp16, HF backend, `max_memory_per_gpu: 22GiB` so they fit **3–4× L40S**.
- **Run path:** `salloc -p gpu -C GPU_SKU:L40S -G 4` → `smoke_l40s.sh 10` → `run_l40s.sh 500` (see `l40s_session/MANUAL.md`).

### Option A — works right now (HF transformers, fp16, no install)
| Optimizer + Evaluator | ~VRAM | Fits 48 GB? |
|---|---|---|

### Option B — bigger + faster on the *same* single card (needs a vLLM install)
The L40S is Ada (sm_89), which **vLLM supports natively with AWQ 4-bit** — and AWQ sidesteps the broken bitsandbytes. If we install a **torch-2.6-compatible vLLM** (an older pin; the latest won't build here), one L40S could host:
- **32B-AWQ optimizer (~20 GB) + 14B-AWQ evaluator (~9 GB) ≈ 30 GB** on this single 48 GB card.
- Plus vLLM is **~5–10× faster** than HF (paged attention / batching) — which matters a lot because the agentic loop is generation-heavy.

This is the **highest value-per-card path**: near the original ~32B quality target on *one* L40S, much faster. Risk: the vLLM install fought us before; on this newer node with the right version pin it's worth a ~30–60 min attempt.

### Not possible on one L40S
- **fp16 32B pair, Mixtral-8x22B, or Llama-70B** — these need the multi-GPU allocation (the one we just cancelled) or an H100, regardless of backend.
- 4-bit via **bitsandbytes** — broken on this el7 env; AWQ-via-vLLM is the only working quantization route.

def is_cardiovascular(code, version) -> bool:
    c = str(code)
    if int(version) == 10:
        if not c.startswith("I"):
            return False
        return not ("I60" <= c[:3] <= "I69")
    try:
        n = int(c[:3])
    except ValueError:
        return False
    return (390 <= n <= 459) and not (430 <= n <= 438)
